clinicalPearls: Characterised by spontaneous, painless, continuous superficial peeling of the outer skin, often leaving no scarring
An acral form (limited to hands and feet) is caused by TGM5 mutations, while a generalised inflammatory form is caused by CDSN (corneodesmosin) mutations
The generalised inflammatory type is associated with erythroderma, pruritus and atopic features and can resemble Netherton syndrome
Peeling is superficial (within the stratum corneum/granular layer), distinguishing it from the deeper blistering of epidermolysis bullosa
The Nikolsky-like separation is at a more superficial plane than in immunobullous or staphylococcal scalded-skin disease
Autosomal recessive inheritance; onset is usually at or soon after birth or in early childhood
Management is supportive with emollients, gentle skin care and avoidance of friction; no curative therapy exists
reference.pathophysiology: Peeling skin syndrome comprises autosomal recessive disorders of the cornified layer characterised by loss of cohesion between corneocytes at a superficial epidermal plane. The localised acral form is caused by mutations in TGM5, which encodes transglutaminase 5, an enzyme that cross-links structural proteins of the cornified cell envelope; its deficiency weakens the envelope so that the stratum corneum detaches from the underlying epidermis. The generalised inflammatory form results from mutations in CDSN encoding corneodesmosin, an adhesive component of corneodesmosomes that holds corneocytes together; loss of corneodesmosin causes separation high in the epidermis with associated barrier failure, inflammation and allergic sensitisation. In both, the split occurs superficially, giving painless peeling without deep blistering.
additionalDifferentials: Acral peeling from friction or exogenous causes
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of TGM5 and CDSN
Assessment for erythroderma, atopy and raised IgE in the generalised form
Examination of hair to help exclude Netherton syndrome
Microbiological swabs to exclude staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome
redFlags: Extensive erythroderma with barrier failure, fluid loss or infection in infancy
Failure to thrive in the generalised inflammatory form
Recurrent skin infection from a compromised barrier
Features suggesting Netherton syndrome requiring reappraisal
reference.prognosis: Peeling skin syndrome is a chronic condition, but the localised acral form is generally mild and compatible with normal health, while the generalised inflammatory form can cause more troublesome erythroderma, itch and barrier problems. It is not life-limiting in most cases, though symptoms persist and require ongoing supportive care.
pitfalls: Confusing the generalised form with Netherton syndrome or atopic erythroderma
Interpreting superficial peeling as epidermolysis bullosa and over-investigating for deep blistering
Mistaking it for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and giving unnecessary treatment
Failing to distinguish the acral (TGM5) from the generalised (CDSN) form for counselling
